clue.text: Fast asleep, exactly as everyone understands it

parts.note: dead means exactly, as in dead centre or dead on time
something put to the world is put to everyone, so the phrase means to all as they see it

explanation.surface: Someone sound asleep is described in terms that everybody would recognise.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue splits into DEAD (exactly) and a phrase meaning in everyone's terms, which together give the idiom for sleeping soundly.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone so deeply asleep that nothing around them registers, an informal synonym for sound slumber.

clue.text: In end of a street, oddly projecting from window

indicators.note: oddly means strangely arranged, so the letters are reshuffled

parts.note: used as written
used as written
used as written
used as written
used as written

explanation.surface: Something juts out of a window at the end of a road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' rearranges the fourteen letters INENDOFASTREET. 'Projecting' means throwing, not jutting out.
explanation.definitionFit: The act of hurling someone or something out through a window, from the Latin for window.

clue.text: Entrance of one of Lydia's suitors, say

indicators.note: say tells us the phrase is to be heard spoken, giving a word that sounds like it

parts.note: Lydia Languish's suitors in Sheridan's play The Rivals compete for her, so one of them is a rival

explanation.surface: One of the men courting Lydia makes his entrance.
explanation.walkthrough: Lydia Languish is the heroine of Sheridan's comedy The Rivals; spoken, 'a rival' matches the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An entrance is a coming in, the moment of reaching a place.

clue.text: Riding equipment youngsters initially viewed as shoddy

parts.note: tack is the saddle, bridle and other gear for riding a horse

indicators.note: initially means only the first letter of youngsters is used

explanation.surface: Children looked at horse gear and thought it cheap.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheap and tasteless, of poor quality, is a synonym for shabby.

clue.text: Give cutter an order to do this?

definitions.text: Give cutter an order to do this?

parts.words: Give cutter an order to do this?
parts.note: a cutter is a boat, but read as one who cuts, the order to give would be to shorten something

explanation.surface: A ship's captain wonders what command to issue to a small vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: A cutter is a small sailing ship; here it is read as a person whose job is to cut, told to cut something short.
explanation.definitionFit: To shorten by cutting off a part is exactly what a cutter does when ordered.

clue.text: Surveying instrument's first lost, but still surviving

indicators.note: first lost says the opening letter of the instrument is dropped

parts.note: a sextant is an instrument for measuring angles, used in surveying and navigation

explanation.surface: An old navigation tool loses a part but continues to exist.
explanation.definitionFit: Of a document or species, still in existence rather than lost, a synonym for remaining.

clue.text: White rose propagated under different conditions

indicators.note: propagated, as of plants bred anew, means the letters are rearranged

parts.note: used as written
used as written

explanation.surface: A gardener has grown a pale bloom from a cutting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'propagated' rearranges WHITEROSE.
explanation.definitionFit: If things were not so, or in other circumstances, is the sense of this adverb.

clue.text: Oil producer's love upset offspring

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means turned upside down, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: love means nil, a zero score in tennis
seed means offspring, descendants

explanation.surface: A love affair upsets the children of a man who drills for oil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns NIL into LIN.
explanation.definitionFit: The seed of flax is pressed for an oil used in paints and varnishes, so it is an oil source.

clue.text: Fail one's colleagues, but prepare cot for use

definitions.meaning: to disappoint your team by underperforming
literally to lower the drop side of a baby's cot so it can be used

explanation.definitionFit: Disappointing one's team-mates is the idiom; lowering a cot's hinged rail is the literal reading.

clue.text: Enclosed area crew captured, it's said

indicators.note: it's said tells us the words are to be heard spoken, so they give a word that sounds the same

parts.note: a rowing four is a crew and captured means caught, so the phrase is four caught

explanation.surface: A crew is reported to have been taken prisoner.
explanation.definitionFit: The paved area in front of a building or a garage, bounded by it, is an enclosed space before the main structure.

clue.text: Rotatable joint inserted in thigh ingeniously

indicators.note: inserted in says the answer sits within the following words, spanning the gap between them

explanation.surface: Someone has cleverly fitted an artificial pivoting joint into a thigh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inserted in' points to the run of letters inside 'thigh ingeniously': tHIGH INGEniously.
explanation.definitionFit: A door or lid swings on this pivoting fitting, a joint that lets one part rotate against another.

clue.text: Hard worker opposed to being in service

indicators.note: being in says one piece sits inside another, here the short letter inside the armed service

parts.note: the navy is one of the armed services
V stands for versus, meaning opposed to, as in a sports fixture

explanation.surface: A diligent worker objects to being enlisted in the forces.
explanation.walkthrough: A navvy is a British labourer, originally one who dug canals ('navigations').
explanation.definitionFit: A labourer doing heavy digging work on roads or railways is a byword for someone who toils physically.

clue.text: Agreeing to study game with. fellow outside

parts.note: to con is an old word meaning to study or learn by heart

indicators.note: outside says the fellow goes round the game, enclosing it

parts.note: a gent is a gentleman, a fellow
RU is rugby union, a ball game

explanation.surface: Someone consents to examine a sport alongside a man who is not involved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' is only a link; 'outside' tells the fellow to wrap around the game. CON for study is an old usage solvers meet often in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: In geometry and general use it means matching or in harmony, so it is a synonym for corresponding.

clue.text: Immoral behaviour regrettably.. backed by business community.

indicators.note: backed means turned back to front, so the word for regrettably is read in reverse

parts.note: alas is an exclamation used to mean regrettably or sadly
the City is London's financial district, home of its business community

explanation.surface: Bad conduct is sadly being funded by the commercial world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backed by' reads like 'supported by' in the surface, but 'backed' turns the sigh round. The City is London's financial centre.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewdness or lechery is a kind of improper conduct, especially of a sexual nature.

clue.text: Cleans out jumble in diplomat's residence

indicators.note: jumble means mix up, so the letters are put in a new order

parts.note: used as written
used as written

explanation.surface: Someone tidies up the clutter in an ambassador's home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jumble' rearranges CLEANSOUT.
explanation.definitionFit: The official premises of a consul, a diplomat representing a state abroad.

clue.text: Porridge that is something below par

parts.note: porridge is British slang for a prison sentence, as is bird (from rhyming slang bird-lime, time)
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, meaning that is

explanation.surface: The breakfast cereal is said to be not quite up to standard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Porridge' is not oats here but British slang for time in prison, also called BIRD.
explanation.definitionFit: In golf a hole completed in one stroke fewer than the standard score is a sub-par result.

clue.text: Flower once known upriver

parts.note: wist is the archaic past tense of wit, to know
the river Aire, in Yorkshire, read upward in this down clue

explanation.surface: A bloom once grew farther up the river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Aire is a river in Yorkshire; in a down clue 'upriver' reads it from bottom to top, ERIA.
explanation.definitionFit: A climbing plant with hanging clusters of lilac blooms, an example of a flowering plant.

clue.text: Traveller in the Orient appears to be discontented

parts.note: a rep, a sales representative, is a commercial traveller
the Orient is the East, abbreviated E

explanation.surface: A salesman working in the Far East seems unhappy.
explanation.definitionFit: To fret or complain inwardly is to feel dissatisfied, a literary synonym for being unhappy.

clue.text: Obtain water-container to accommodate churchman

indicators.note: to accommodate means to hold within, so the churchman goes inside the container

parts.note: a pail is a bucket for water
Rev, short for Reverend, is a clergyman

explanation.surface: A bucket is needed to fit in a vicar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Obtain' is not to get here but the intransitive sense of to be in force, as in 'the rule still obtains'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean to be established or in general use, as a custom that holds sway.

clue.text: Scholars settled down a long time before it returned

parts.note: lit, as of a bird that has alighted, means settled down
an era is a long period of time

indicators.note: returned means the little word it comes back the other way round

explanation.surface: Academics took a long time to settle before it came back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'settled down' is the past tense of alight, as a bird landing; 'returned' turns the little word round, and 'before' just orders the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Learned people collectively, the literary intelligentsia, are men and women of letters.

clue.text: Canines may have their fill of it

definitions.text: Canines may have their fill of it

parts.words: Canines may have their fill of it
parts.note: canines suggests dogs eating their fill, but the teeth may be filled with a dental alloy

explanation.surface: Dogs are allowed to eat as much as they like.
explanation.walkthrough: Canines here are teeth, and their fill is a filling.
explanation.definitionFit: A mercury alloy has long been used by dentists to fill cavities in teeth.

clue.text: Spirits in glasses

definitions.meaning: ghosts or phantoms of the dead

explanation.definitionFit: Shades are ghosts in literary use and sunglasses in slang.

clue.text: It supported men investing in cert, but he went bust

indicators.note: went bust means broke apart, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: used as written
used as written
used as written

explanation.surface: A gambler backed a racing certainty and lost everything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'went bust' rearranges CERTBUTHE. 'Investing' here means besieging, not putting money in.
explanation.definitionFit: This medieval siege catapult backed up soldiers besieging a castle by hurling missiles at its walls.

clue.text: Smooth woman 'with American backing

indicators.note: backing means going in reverse, here over both the woman and the American

parts.note: Eva is a woman's name

explanation.surface: A suave woman is supported by an American.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns EVAUS around as a whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Polished and urbane in manner, a charming person is smooth-mannered.

clue.text: Tailor, we hear, steps over fence

indicators.note: we hear says the word is to be heard, so it gives one spelt differently but sounding alike

parts.note: to style, as with hair or clothes, is to tailor or fashion

explanation.surface: A dressmaker apparently climbs over a fence.
explanation.definitionFit: Steps or a bar built so walkers can climb across a boundary are a rural crossing point.

clue.text: Honour attracting expression of triumph in US city

parts.note: the OM, Order of Merit, is a British honour
aha is an exclamation of triumph or discovery

explanation.surface: A recipient of a decoration cries out in delight in an American city.
explanation.walkthrough: The OM (Order of Merit) is an honour awarded by the British monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: A city in Nebraska on the Missouri River, an example of an American urban centre.

clue.text: Bold action, blundering into casual retirement

indicators.note: into says the first piece goes inside the second
retirement means drawing back, so the word for casual is read in reverse

parts.note: odd means casual or occasional, as in odd jobs
erring means making mistakes, blundering

explanation.surface: Someone stumbles into an informal retirement in a daring act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retirement' looks like the definition's partner but turns the word for casual round, making DDO; 'into' then places the blunder inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Heroic courage shown in deeds, an old-fashioned term for daring exploits.

clue.text: Senior politician, say, admitted by presbyter's servant

indicators.note: admitted by says the word for say is taken inside the presbyter's servant

parts.note: a presbyter is an elder of the church, so presbyter's gives elder's
to state means to say
a man is a manservant

explanation.surface: A senior politician is quoted as being let in by a church elder's attendant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' looks like the usual signal for an example, but here it is a verb meaning declare, fitted into the presbyter's servant.
explanation.definitionFit: A veteran politician respected for experience and wisdom is a senior figure in government.
